sop_steps.action: Get the clinic's pack list and instrument counts before quoting a single instrument.
sop_steps.detail: Use the Texas A&M generals pack as the template: four Allis, three Carmalts, three Kelly or Crile, four mosquitoes, one needle holder, three scissors, towel clamps, Brown-Adsons, spay hook, blade handle [PEER at TAMU — WoO-cNElJpg @ 00:03:20].

sop_steps.title: Quote the full reprocessing chain
sop_steps.action: Attach wash tubs, nylon and steel brushes, ultrasonic cleaner, and surgical milk to every instrument order.
sop_steps.detail: The workflow requires nylon brushes for smooth surfaces, steel brushes for jaws and teeth, about 10 minutes ultrasonic, and about a minute in milk [Vet Candy | Veterinary Education, CE & News — Zb4YYmRy5x0 @ 00:09:37].

sop_steps.title: Inspect, refurbish, and leak test used units
sop_steps.action: Certify used equipment before listing it, and pressure test every flexible scope on intake.
sop_steps.detail: Used veterinary equipment sells when thoroughly inspected and refurbished by a reliable provider [MFI Medical — jzPWxnzAds0 @ 00:01:09]; pump scopes to the test area and watch the gauge hold before submersion [Surgical Direct (Surgical Direct) — DrTCjk0roNk @ 00:06:42].

sop_steps.title: Price ASC offers against cost per case
sop_steps.action: Present savings per case against the center's reimbursement, with backup trays staged rather than opened.
sop_steps.detail: Ballard's center compares each surgeon's total knee cost, targets savings like 750 dollars per case, and keeps one backup tray and two cable systems unopened outside the room [American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons — AQIyPCz9bJM @ 00:26:08].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Pack-wrapping protocol is the first place clinic buyers split, and it dictates how much wrap, tape, and tray inventory each practice burns. Dr. Cathy Kelly at Four Paws Animal Hospital in Fredericksburg double wraps most surgical packs in cloth drapes, snugs them with plain painter's tape, and relies on one strip of indicator tape plus an internal indicator strip [PlDJXzo7cN4 @ 00:02:47]. Rachel Romo, head orthopedic surgical technician at Texas A&M Small Animal Hospital, triple wraps instead: a towel innermost, a paper drape that lets steam and pressure in but keeps air and moisture out afterward, and a cloth outer wrap, with unused triple-wrapped packs rewashed, repacked, and resterilized every six months [WoO-cNElJpg @ 00:20:10]. Dr. Armstrong at Forever Family Animal Hospital runs two layers so a pack can be handed off sterilely, closes it with regular masking tape, and drops an okay strip near the instruments as the final sterility marker [1jEOjg29-e0 @ 00:09:27]. Alyssa Mages at Vet Candy specs blue paper-like Gemini wrap for inner and outer layers on orthopedic and soft tissue sets, two small cloth wraps for small sets, and double pouches for gelpies and bone rasps [Zb4YYmRy5x0 @ 00:11:38]. Wrap count, tape habit, and shelf-life rule all change the consumable basket a clinic reorders.

Reprocessing chemistry and hardware budgets diverge just as hard. Romo soaks dirty instruments in an enzymatic product for at least 10 minutes, scrubs finger rings and box locks, then dunks everything in instrument milk, a lubricant that keeps steel from drying out and rusting after steam sterilization [WoO-cNElJpg @ 00:01:52]. Mages layers in more equipment: a plastic tub inside the sink so surgical stainless never sits in a steel sink, nylon brushes for smooth surfaces and steel brushes for serrated jaws, about 10 minutes in an ultrasonic cleaner, then roughly a minute in the milk bath [Zb4YYmRy5x0 @ 00:09:55]. On hardware, LopinMoetas pitches dental clinics on AliExpress sterilization containers ranging from a $5.23 heat-resistant bur soaking box to a roughly $21 silicone-mat tray rated five stars by over 4,800 buyers [8kG0BUAGcP4 @ 00:00:33]. Dr. Armstrong takes the premium position on the instruments themselves, calling them very expensive, insisting they be cared for, sharpened, and special ordered, and running German surgical instruments that can last decades with real care [1jEOjg29-e0 @ 00:10:19]. Buyers in this vertical sit on both ends: commodity trays, cassettes, and bur holders on one side, sharpened premium steel on the other.

ASC operators disagree over how to build a center and how lean to run it. Dr. James Ballard of the Oregon Surgical Institute started outpatient totals about eight years ago in a small sports ASC with an outside consulting service, then brought in Zimmer Biomet's Accelero for a de novo location built for spine and total joints, calling it quite different, more holistic, and the hands-down choice of a group of rival surgeons who do not even share implants [AQIyPCz9bJM @ 00:03:36]. Ballard credits the efficient care program with cutting total knee trays from five to two, a change even a huge sterile processing department appreciates because nobody is cleaning five trays [AQIyPCz9bJM @ 00:23:06]. Erica Smith, Surgical Solutions manager at Henry Schein, pulls a different lever: single-use devices go into bins, ship to Provision, get inspected, tested, and sterilized twice as much as the FDA requires, and come back for reuse, which also protects against back orders [VMonxNBLqE4 @ 00:04:27]. MFI Medical gives veterinary buyers a qualified yes on used equipment, as long as units are thoroughly inspected and refurbished by a reliable seller, and sells its own certified used units [jzPWxnzAds0 @ 00:01:23]. Reuse, refurbishment, and new standardized kits all compete for the same ASC and clinic budget.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Flexible endoscopes are the costliest failure point here, and Joe, clinical operations manager at Surgical Direct, maps exactly where they break. Letting the scope hit a hard floor can damage any portion of it, and the soft bending rubber at the tip is easily cut by a sharp instrument or an animal's tooth [DrTCjk0roNk @ 00:01:20]. Joe calls leak testing the most important part of scope care: lock the leak tester onto the soaking cap, pump until the gauge sits in the test area, confirm it does not drop for a few seconds, then submerge, because catching a leak early is the difference between a complete rebuild and a small bending rubber repair [DrTCjk0roNk @ 00:06:24]. Sequencing errors fake the result. Adding enzymatic cleaner before the leak test fills the water with bubbles and produces a false positive, and failing to flush every channel of air does the same; genuine leaks usually look like champagne bubbles [DrTCjk0roNk @ 00:08:18]. MFI Medical applies the same leak discipline to anesthesia equipment, listing leak checks, proper calibration, and the manufacturer's upkeep guidelines as the baseline for safe operation [jzPWxnzAds0 @ 00:01:40]. Any scope or anesthesia unit moving through resale lives or dies on these checks.

Sterile-processing mistakes show up as scrapped packs, rusted steel, torn pouches, and retained gauze. Romo at Texas A&M wears a bouffant while washing, packing, and wrapping because a hair found in a pack, whether anyone calls it sterile hair or not, means passing that pack off and pulling a new one [WoO-cNElJpg @ 00:10:54]. Mages warns that instruments left in the ultrasonic cleaner or the milk bath overnight will rust, so the cycle has to be finished by whoever started it rather than left for somebody else [Zb4YYmRy5x0 @ 00:10:28]. Pouches fail when curved instruments such as mosquitoes go in curve-down and punch through the paper, so curves face the plastic side, handles go in first, and delicate or sharp items get double pouched in case they poke through the first layer [Zb4YYmRy5x0 @ 00:11:55]. Dr. Armstrong attacks the worst outcome, retained sponges, by counting radio-opaque blue-lined gauze before and after surgery and sometimes shooting a post-op x-ray to confirm nothing remains in the abdomen [1jEOjg29-e0 @ 00:08:21]. Every one of these failures maps to a consumable these practitioners keep stocked: bouffants, instrument milk, correctly sized pouches, and radio-opaque gauze.

The money traps sit in compliance, contracts, and cost-per-case math. Brett Coffin, founder of Nuronus, points to Gums Dental Care, a solo dental practice fined seventy thousand dollars with no breach and no ransomware, purely because a patient asked for records and the office missed HIPAA's deadline; OCR collected almost ten million dollars across twenty-two enforcement actions in 2024 [iAwNQ3QON9c @ 00:00:24]. Jimmy of AI Training Data Broker watches clinic data deals die the moment an AI lab's lawyer asks which contract allows AI training and nobody at the clinic can answer, usually because a software vendor contract signed years earlier holds a secondary use clause nobody tracked [p2c6HcivkAA @ 00:00:02]. On the ASC side, Ballard turns per-surgeon cost reports into action, asking why a blade costs $85 when the center could get it for $45, and learning the answer was simply that nobody asked [AQIyPCz9bJM @ 00:26:08]. Ballard and Pickering both frame $750 in per-case savings as paramount when squeezing a Medicare knee into roughly $8,400 of reimbursement, tying it directly to the survival of the surgery center [AQIyPCz9bJM @ 00:26:27]. Margins that thin punish any vendor who cannot justify a line item.

callout.title: Four Checks Before Any Clinic Deal Closes
callout.body: Each gate below is a failure a named practitioner reported firsthand or warned about. Clear all four before quoting, shipping, or onboarding a clinic buyer.
items: Scope intake: inspect the distal end and bending rubber for floor-impact damage and tooth or instrument cuts, then pressure-test before any immersion [Surgical Direct (Surgical Direct) — DrTCjk0roNk @ 00:01:04].

Pack release: confirm the outer indicator tape shows black stripes and the inner indicator strip changed before any pack leaves processing [Four Paws Animal Hospital & Wellness Center — PlDJXzo7cN4 @ 00:03:52].
Records clock: dental clients must answer patient record requests inside HIPAA's deadline, since Gums Dental Care was fined seventy thousand dollars with no breach [Nuronus — iAwNQ3QON9c @ 00:00:24].
Data contracts: locate the software vendor contract's secondary use clause before any AI lab call, or the deal sits for weeks [AI Training Data Broker — p2c6HcivkAA @ 00:00:23].

action_checklist: Pressure-test every flexible scope with the hand pump before adding any enzymatic cleaner, then flush all channels of air so bubbles cannot fake a leak [Surgical Direct (Surgical Direct) — DrTCjk0roNk @ 00:08:18].

Label every wrapped pack with department, contents, date, and the initials of whoever washed, packed, and wrapped it, and reprocess triple-wrapped packs left unused for six months [PEER at TAMU — WoO-cNElJpg @ 00:20:10].

Pull instruments from the ultrasonic cleaner and the roughly one-minute milk bath the same session, never overnight, to prevent rust [Vet Candy | Veterinary Education, CE & News — Zb4YYmRy5x0 @ 00:10:28].

chapters.question_prompt: How is medical capital equipment sold, priced, and reimbursed, and who captures the profit?
chapters.title: Selling Medical Equipment: Sales Careers and Industry Economics
chapters.subtitle: Capital equipment sales tactics, long hospital sales cycles, breaking into device sales, rep skills and career paths, pricing and reimbursement, Medicare DME coverage, who profits from hospital technology, device industry economics, software license traps, and a dialysis deployment case study
chapters.executive_summary: Device sales veterans agree the job is won through referrals, not online applications. Valente says almost all roles come from referrals and fewer than 1% of applicants break in, and Jacob got a call four weeks before a posting went live. Once inside, the consensus is to educate rather than pitch, accept roughly six months of thin selling, and treat capital as a one-to-five-year campaign run through champions, VAC members and CFO ROI models. The street mechanics are precise: no-note LinkedIn requests, sub-100-word messages, 70/30 listening ratios, and Licata's funnel of 30 accounts for one or two purchase orders. On the economics side, practitioners treat the machine as the opening move, with service contracts, consumables and utilization driving recurring revenue. They split on pay structures, entry paths, paid coaching programs and whether capital is reachable for beginners.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every recruiter-side voice converges on one rule: the job is won through people, not portals. Vincent Valente of Break Into Medical Device Sales, who broke in at 23 and ranked #1 of 109 reps, states that almost all jobs are landed from referrals and that fewer than 1% of applicants make it into the field [-KxAlnmN4IY @ 00:18:27]. Jacob of New to Medical Device Sales goes further: don't apply online at all, because AI screening filters applicants and many postings are already filled; Jacob got a call four weeks before the role was even posted [G5Dl1131xAw @ 00:43:20]. Matt of Med Sales With Matt builds the same funnel from the bottom, targeting Area Sales Managers, hiring managers, recruiters, Regional Sales Directors and territory managers, and insists on giving something before asking [2Nn9rL0ZXRg @ 00:02:30]. Rachel Keaton of Medical Sales U is the street-level proof: she reached out to 20 device companies, got a scrub tech's rep's cell number, took that rep to coffee, and walked up to the hiring director at his hotel with no appointment and walked away with the job [15ffob3rfCw @ 00:17:58]. The shared baseline is persistence plus warm access, because cold online applications sink against 200 to 400 applicants per opening.

On the selling floor, trust beats pitching and the first six months are a build phase. Keaton admits she sold very little for her first six months, notes that capital takes about six months to build momentum anyway, and calls performance a lagging indicator of behaviors [15ffob3rfCw @ 00:24:35]. Jacob's panel tells new reps not to try to sell for six months; the 90-day goal is that staff know who you are and where your trays are kept, then you prove yourself over 12 months without love bombing [G5Dl1131xAw @ 01:05:42]. Joe Licata frames capital the same way: keep educating rather than selling, and count simply getting access inside the hospital on your first visit as a win [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:28:55]. The 2026 reality check from Break Into Medical Device Sales agrees that you win by being reliable, knowledgeable and professional, not pushy, because this is not a 45-minute close [fHUIy8gtER4 @ 00:07:37]. The cycle lengths explain the patience: Keaton sees capital cycles from one to two months up to one to two years depending on how important the hospital thinks the product is, Vince quotes six months to two years on deals from 50 to a million dollars plus, and Licata has carried deals open three years that never closed.

The economics consensus is that the box is only the opening move. The Business Beneath walks a fictional $1M purchase that carries another $200,000 for facility prep and installation before maintenance, software, repairs and training, calls it total cost of ownership, and notes that maintenance agreements create recurring revenue for manufacturers [iWKTCfxvEUg @ 00:04:20]. Industry Games puts numbers on the consumables model: a monitor selling for ₹1 lakh against ₹60K cost, a sensor at ₹400 against ₹150, and ₹5.25 lakh in sensor gross profit over seven years plus an 8% AMC, with retraining and compatibility locking the customer in [je3P4ran5jk @ 00:08:04]. Licata closes the loop from the rep side: after the close, drive utilization so the equipment does not sit collecting dust [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:57:31]. Pay structure tracks that deal shape. Vince lays out capital as the highest base with the lowest commission upside because transactions are rare, disposables as a 40 to 70k base with 10 to 20 thousand dollars a month possible in commissions, and implants as $1K to 50K cases billed the same day with high base and uncapped commission [IaALQ3iuJp8 @ 00:02:42]. Valente adds that the roles are mostly W-2, so the upside sits on top of a salaried base.

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The networking machine runs on hard numbers. Jacob's rule for LinkedIn connection requests is blunt: 'For the love of God, do not send a note,' because Jacob rejects 70%+ of noted requests and notes cap at 300 characters anyway; one example ran 70 sent for 20 accepted, while Ryan saw roughly 50% acceptance [G5Dl1131xAw @ 00:30:02]. Follow-up messages stay under about 100 words or three paragraphs, ask for a 5 to 10 minute call 'to learn,' and include a phone number. Matt logs every call and number in an Excel spreadsheet and sets a phone reminder to follow up in about a week, and he flags the 'open to work' badge as desperation [2Nn9rL0ZXRg @ 00:01:35]. On the calls themselves, Jacob's diagnostic is that 40 calls with zero interviews usually means you talked only about yourself, the 'first date' problem, and the phrase 'pick your brain' is banned from outreach [9bfKQdKe_vU @ 00:18:20]. The fix is a 70/30 talking ratio with the contact doing most of the talking, calls that compound on each other, and ironclad answers to the four Y's: why med device, why that company, why that division, why you, where 'to make money' is a worthless answer [G5Dl1131xAw @ 00:46:16].

Capital deals run on a mapped committee, and Licata names the seats: champion physician, supporting physicians, VAC members, the department VP, CFO, CEO, CNO and materials management. Reps are barred from the VAC, so the physician presents, and Licata schedules an in-service a day or a couple of days before that meeting [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:11:33]. Anything above $150K needs approval outside the department; Licata's own example was a $2.2M+ robotic ablation system plus a $2M lab build-out, nearly $5M total, which is why the rep must change hats, talking clinical outcomes to physicians and ROI models to the CFO [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:16:12]. Keaton's sequence matches: educate the physician, confirm the issue matters enough to take to leadership, then meet the CEO, CFO and COO, all while carrying the physician's personal story of why they entered the field through every meeting [15ffob3rfCw @ 00:23:12]. The pipeline math is brutal: 30 accounts yield one or two purchase orders, so Licata tracks 5 to 20 CRM stages such as champion, C-suite meeting, site visit and construction project, uses impending dates like construction to create urgency, and treats budget and champion as the two universals [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:37:42].

Face-to-face with surgeons, the tactics are scripted. Jacob's question sequence is: what are you using, how long, and since residency, because a residency-trained user usually just didn't want to change, while someone who switched is open to change, so ask why they switched; at the scrub sink with 30 seconds, skip rapport and go straight to needs [PaW-3LfksaU @ 00:06:09]. Since doctors rarely admit struggles, reference 'Dr B' and ask if they've dealt with the same problem. When a gatekeeper gives the doctor only four minutes, Jacob's panel offers to reschedule, and after paying for a $300 lunch they ask for the next meeting and close for a next step [G5Dl1131xAw @ 01:14:35]. Licata scales the same play: department lunches can feed 60 to 70 people, and he has stayed four hours fact-finding [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:49:08]. In disposables, targeting is volume math. Vince's example is an electrosurgical device at 'five to $700' sold in boxes of five, aimed at high-volume bariatric surgeons doing five cases a day, and Vince calls disposables the best entry point despite being commoditized and price-driven [IaALQ3iuJp8 @ 00:08:21]. Rehearse any presentation out loud 10 to 12 times before delivering it.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over which lane a newcomer should attack first. Vince of Break Into Medical Device Sales calls disposables the best entry point, warns that capital is one of the hardest lanes to crack without prior device experience, and says Intuitive rarely hires outsiders for capital seats [IaALQ3iuJp8 @ 00:05:59]. Joe Licata backs that gate from the capital side, framing $500K-plus capital equipment as a promotable role that demands earlier device or pharma time inside hospitals [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:02:21]. Rachel Keaton of Medical Sales U is the live counterexample: they cold-contacted 20 device companies, landed coffee with a scrub tech's rep, and finally approached the hiring director at his hotel with no appointment and landed the capital job [15ffob3rfCw @ 00:19:22]. On implants, Vince openly rejects their own infographic's hardest-to-break-into label, insisting plenty of implant jobs suit beginners, and pushes a get-in-where-you-can-get-in rule because you can pivot once the exposure sits on your resume. The 2026 video on the same channel adds a time box for that pivot: run ortho for one to two years and then move, because two-to-three-hour surgeries stacked into six-to-eight-hour OR days wear reps down [fHUIy8gtER4 @ 00:04:56].

Practitioners also split on how hard to press once inside the hospital. Rachel Keaton's capital playbook is built around urgency: start with the physician or anyone who will listen, accept that the champion may not be the end user, and make them feel they need the system now, not in a year [15ffob3rfCw @ 00:03:51]. Joe Licata runs the opposite tempo on multi-year capital deals, telling reps to keep educating rather than keep selling while the committee machinery grinds forward [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:28:55]. The 30-60-90 plan is another open fight. Vincent Valente lists it inside phase three of their break-in system, mastering the interviews, after positioning yourself and building an inside network [-KxAlnmN4IY @ 00:18:16]. Licata calls generic 30-60-90s garbage and wants candidates to walk the interviewer through real CRM stages instead, the five to twenty checkpoints such as champion secured, C-suite meeting, site visit, and construction project [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:25:46]. Read together, the operator move is to bring the plan only if it is built from stage-level specifics, and to calibrate pressure to deal size: urgency language for a physician-led purchase, slow education for a nearly $5M robotic ablation build-out that needs sign-off outside the department.

The paid-help question splits the channels most openly, and nearly every voice here also sells a program. Vincent Valente calls the 80 to 90 percent placement claims of med sales colleges misleading and says clients came to them after already paying $20,000 elsewhere [-KxAlnmN4IY @ 00:20:23]. Vince's own channel pitches a Med Device Sales Academy promising placement in 90 days, so the college critique comes from a direct competitor. Matt of Med Sales With Matt frames coaching as cheap leverage, spending roughly $1,000 to land a job that pays over $100,000 [2Nn9rL0ZXRg @ 00:03:42]. Jacob of New to Medical Device Sales pushes hardest, warning that the cheap option ends up being the no option and pricing a $60K step back at roughly three years of lost ground [9bfKQdKe_vU @ 00:29:42]. Yet the same session tells candidates never to skip a 60K role, because multiple offers trigger bidding wars and you can always say no to the job [9bfKQdKe_vU @ 00:25:54]. The operator reconciliation: interview for everything, including low-base and relocation roles such as the Tampa example, but treat offers as leverage rather than automatic acceptances, and weigh any program fee against the base delta it actually buys you.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Capital is where months of work die in a single meeting. Joe Licata lost a three-year deal to a service-agreement objection and puts it bluntly: one comment, literally one comment, destroyed three years of work [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:54:21]. Vince warns that capital reps can pour eight months into an account and watch it fall flat, while the same lane pays the highest base with the lowest commission upside on one or two deals per account per year [IaALQ3iuJp8 @ 00:04:52]. The ramp trap compounds it. Rachel Keaton sold very little for the first six months and notes capital takes about six months to build momentum anyway, insisting performance is a lagging indicator of behaviors such as physician meetings and market-development dinners [15ffob3rfCw @ 00:24:35]. Licata's warning is that some companies still demand closed sales within three to six months, so a new hire has to confirm a realistic timeline with the hiring manager up front [KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:06:11]. The economics check: Licata's own funnel runs 30 accounts for one or two purchase orders on a one-to-eighteen-month average cycle, so a six-month quota clock has to be surfaced during the interview loop.

The second failure cluster is the body and the comp plan. The 2026 truth video from Break Into Medical Device Sales says a 7:00 OR start means being up by 4:30 to 5:00, with half your days in the OR after a 30-to-60-minute drive, and calls it not a sleep-in, roll-out-of-bed career [fHUIy8gtER4 @ 00:02:07]. Haley, a Hologic rep, lives the extreme version: their furthest account sits five hours away, and they wake at 2 or 3 a.m. and log some 20-to-21-hour days [G5Dl1131xAw @ 01:00:08]. Exhaustion also derails new hires early. Ryan, now an Intuitive CTA, slept about four hours before a Procept training evaluation that required a 90-plus score, failed it, and left after six weeks [G5Dl1131xAw @ 00:10:39]. Then there is corporate red tape on pay. The same 2026 host reports commission caps, rates lowered after a strong year, and legal and compliance review, and says they beat quota by seven figures yet were underpaid [fHUIy8gtER4 @ 00:06:15]. The economics check is to read the comp plan for caps and rate-reset language before celebrating an OTE number, and to map real drive time across the territory before accepting a rural patch where hospitals sit two hours apart.

On the business side, the failure modes are utilization, cash timing, and pricing you cannot undo. The Business Beneath notes an idle machine still burns space, financing, and maintenance, and that utilization strongly drives cost per examination [iWKTCfxvEUg @ 00:10:35], and Joe Licata separately pushes reps to drive usage after close so equipment does not sit collecting dust. Industry Games models the death spiral: a 40 million rupee loan, 30 percent utilization, 150-day payments, and FX pressure on chips, concluding that debt, low utilization, and delayed payments together wipe out the cash keeping the company alive [je3P4ran5jk @ 00:14:08]. Hidden Industries shows vendor lock-in cutting against hospitals on software: 10,000 seats bought, 4,000 deployed, 6,000 auto-renewed, and a free add-on that raised maintenance 20 percent for three years [uNFHZlCznIw @ 00:04:40]. On price, Tom at Fast Forward Medical Innovation warns that a launch price sets a perception that rarely repositions, and admits underpricing Epivir amid the AZT controversy left arguably about a billion dollars on the table over the product lifetime [oAV1SBup8Q8 @ 00:33:42]. The operator check: model utilization, receivables, and the full total cost of ownership before quoting, never price at the full incremental cost with zero headroom, and audit every renewal for shelfware.

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before You Prospect, Pitch, or Price
callout.body: Every item below is a loss or rejection practitioners hit or watched happen. Clear all four before running outreach, reporting pipeline, or setting a launch price.
items: Never inflate pipeline progress; managers take it as gospel straight to the board, and a single bad comment can still erase three years of work [Joe Licata | Medical Sales Coach — KsMhJhbA73k @ 00:34:00].
Strip the dashes AI leaves in outreach text before sending; it is the number one complaint Jacob hears from hiring managers [New to Medical Device Sales — G5Dl1131xAw @ 00:35:06].
Remove the LinkedIn open to work badge; hiring managers read it as desperation [Med Sales With Matt — 2Nn9rL0ZXRg @ 00:03:11].
Never price at the full $20K incremental cost of the problem you solve; it leaves no headroom for payers [Fast Forward Medical Innovation – Commercialization Education — oAV1SBup8Q8 @ 00:34:59].
